utterances.text: What I didn't get in the course, I made a point of looking it up in some American military handbooks that I had access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to briefly focus on one aspect of the training that you did receive, I believe, before your deployment to the region. Am I correct that during your briefings in Canada you were advised of the existence of storage sites of ammunition in each locality in Bosnia due to the nature of their Territorial Defence concept?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that the briefing did not, however, include information about the precise locations of such stores of munitions?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, because it was considered a different security level than we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to call up a portion of your testimony from the Galic proceedings. It's going to be 65 ter 1D00428, and it should be page 29 in e-court if my notes are accurate. And this should be transcript page 9437. I see it is. And with respect to your answer to the question there about ammunition dumps, you say: "I don't know about the exact location of ammunition depots. I do know that in my preparatory briefing in Canada, we were advised that there was enough ammunition in the stocks of the Yugoslav home defence forces for this war to be carried on for 40 years." Sir, can you affirm this prior testimony of yours to be true and correct as to the information given to you in Canada about the quantities of munitions stored in the stocks of the Yugoslav home defence forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I can, although I can't divulge the source. It was an intelligence source.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, I appreciate that, although I caution we need to have a space between my question and your answer. If we can also scroll down on the -- on the bottom of this page. I'd like to -- I'd like to ask about something that you went on to give information about, starting at line 12, and I will read into the record the question and your answer: "Q. Witness, when you use the expression in English 'the Yugoslav home defence forces,' are you referring to what was known as the Territorial Defence? "A. It -- yes. It is the concept that there was a manoeuvre army which would manoeuvre around the Yugoslavs who defended their own home locality after they had served their conscription -- conscript time. To make this possible on the Swiss model, which I am sure you are familiar with, there was a great series of depots, ammunition storage at the very local level, because the concept rests on the idea that locally trained people can respond to an emergency and defend their own locality without depending on support from outside. This in turn meant that large quantities of small arms ammunition and artillery ammunition for the calibres that we are talking about, 120 millimetre, and even guns and field pieces, would be able in especially an urban area like Sarajevo, which would be a key part of such a concept, because motorised forces would by- pass Sarajevo if it was strongly defended." Sir, again without divulge the identity of the source, could you affirm for us that this selection I have just read from the -- from your prior testimony is true and correct as to the understanding that was given to you before your deployment of the ammunition depots?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me, sir, that unless a party in Sarajevo, or anywhere in Bosnia for that matter, specifically advised you of a location of one of these caches of ammunition, you, in the sense of the UNMO mission, would not have a reason to know about it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, we would not have a reason to know about it unless I had been prior briefed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, sir, that the UNMO mission itself did not task you with investigating the location of such ammo dumps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. The United Nations, as you know, has a practice: They don't engage in intelligence activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that such caches or depots of ammunition could be potentially legitimate military targets depending on where they are located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would agree with the caveat that by the time I arrived I would suspect that all the brigades on both sides had taken out the ammunition from those depots and issued it out to the soldiers and had stored it in a location close to the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would any such locations where ammunition was stored be camouflaged or masked perhaps even in civilian-looking buildings or areas?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, having never been able to discover --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have -- well, perhaps the witness was going to answer, but I'd say it calls for speculation on the part of the witness, would any such locations be camouflaged or masked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can answer that, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. Mr. Ivetic, concern is speculation. Perhaps we ask the witness first whether he has any knowledge about such locations where ammunition may have been stored, be camouflaged or masked. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct, sir, that the UNMO mission did not even suspect any military factories existed within the city of Sarajevo because in your view they did not make military sense?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would say that, yes, our organisation did not suspect there was a functioning military weapons manufacturing plant in Sarajevo because it would be too easily targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that since your time in Sarajevo as a witness in several proceedings before this Tribunal, you now have learned of the existence of the Zrak, Z-r-a-k, factory in Sarajevo which produced optical instruments for sniper weapons?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Has it been brought to your attention in prior proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It has been brought to my attention in prior proceedings, but it doesn't mean I have confirmed it nor believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would such a factory in Sarajevo, which the UNMO mission was unaware of and which you do not confirm, if it did exist, would that be a legitimate target for an opposing military?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you permit, sir, that there could have been other such factories in the Sarajevo and surrounding area that might have been missed and therefore unconfirmed by UNMO and yourself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is it not the essence of that you miss something that you don't know, and to say, Is it possible that you do not know something? I mean every human being who says, It's impossible that I do not know a certain thing, so therefore whether it makes any sense to ask this from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree, and I will withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have knowledge of the Igman factory for ammunition located in Konjic just to the south of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Gorazde, sir, since that was also part of your zone of responsibilities. Do you know or did you know about the Pobjeda factory for ammunition in Gorazde, the one of three that existed in the SFRY ammunition manufacturing industry?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was pointed out a factory which was not functioning which people told me on the ground had been a munition factory, but it certainly wasn't a munitions factory when I saw it. It had holes in the roof.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion in Gorazde to have the Kopaca [phoen], Sopatica [phoen], or Petigor [phoen] location identified for you which was the reserve rear command of the SFRY high command, a significant bunker and command structure?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would such structures, if they existed, be legitimate military targets for an opposing force?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, and if Your Honour would give me the caveat. If it was known, so widely known, why was it not shelled more before I got there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, it seems that you are more or less engaging -- at least you're seeking to engage in a discussion with Mr. Ivetic where you are supposed to answer his questions. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to move to a related topic since we're talking about ammunition. Did you know of the existence of a tunnel that linked the interior of Sarajevo city with the outside of the city under the control of the Bosnian Presidency forces and called the Dobrinja-Butmir tunnel?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I could not confirm it. I sent patrols at both suspected sides and we had great difficulty in getting through Bosnian check-points to confirm anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I appreciate the distinction you're making. Am I correct that although at the time you did not know about it, since then you have gained knowledge that such a tunnel did exist and was used to bring in supplies by the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, if it was a constant complaint that you heard from the Bosnian Serb side that the Bosnian Presidency forces were using tunnels to either bring in weapons, munitions, or trying to outflank the Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. The tunnel allegation was persistently brought up at meetings between both sides and we continually tried to find the entrance and were continually getting stopped and prevented from seeing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this instance, sir, when you say you were continually being stopped and prevented from seeing it, prevented by which opposing force?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: By the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like at this time to call up 65 ter 1D00426.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, sir, I can give you some introductory information. This is a publication entitled "In Harm's Way. The Buck Stops Here: Senior Commanders on Operations," and is edited by a Colonel Bernd Horn. And we see the cover page on the screen now. Sir, are you familiar with this publication?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, contribute an article based -- within this publication?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have just received a note that it's time for the break. I do not know if that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I had two or three minutes on my mind, but if this would be a suitable time then we take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I have a significant amount of questioning on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break, Mr. Thomas of approximately 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 5 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I use the time for the following matter. It relates to Exhibit P6, which was MFI'd on the 16th of July. We heard on the 16th of July that the Prosecution would try to obtain a copy of the document, which is a Security Council Resolution, in a format similar to that of most Security Council Resolutions, and the Chamber would like to be updated by the Prosecution on the matter, not necessarily at this very moment but soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, before the break we had opened up this document. I'd like to now turn to the third page in e-court and ask if you recognise chapter 1 of this publication as an article that you authored based on your experiences in Sarajevo as part of the UNMO mission?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to page 11 of the document and focus on bottom of page 17 of the actual text, which would be the right-hand side of this page in e-court, and address this selection that begins, sir: "Sometimes there are things that you do that fall in an ethical grey area. One such incident involved knowledge of an extensive tunnel system on the front lines. For months my personal reconnaissance on both sides of the line had led me to believe that the Bosnians had constructed a substantial tunnel through which an assault could be mounted on the thinly held Bosnian Serb lines opposite their own. In almost my last days in Sarajevo," and we have to go to the next page, "I was shown this tunnel system by the local commander who knew that I was leaving on my word that I would not divulge the exact location. Curiosity led me to agree. Subsequently, I did indicate to my successor that this was an area requiring careful scrutiny due to the presence of such a tunnel system without giving its precise grid. There were other such incidents involving team members. The commander must be able to live with himself and do what he, or she, thinks is right. There are few who can offer practical advice to the SMO on the matter of ethics." First of all, sir, can I ask you if you can confirm the accuracy and truthfulness of this selection from your article --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again, we have to wait for the translators and the transcript transcribers, so please try to observe a pause. In this article you say that "there were other such incidents involving team members." Could you elaborate for us if these other incidents also involved knowledge of tunnels used by the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: None of the other incidents involved tunnels used by the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And focusing on this incident that you have the personal knowledge of, are you at liberty now to divulge the approximate location of this tunnel system?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do so right now. It's Nedzarici in the -- not too far from the Rainbow Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was there a civilian area nearby or did it pass through a civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The tunnel went underground in no man's land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is there dispute about the location of the tunnel between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm heaving about it for the first time, Your Honours. It's not something that was included in the statement or the article. That's why I asked the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I'm asking whether there is any dispute between Prosecution and Defence about the existence and the location of a tunnel which I understand to be a tunnel under the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a different tunnel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a different tunnel. Then it's good that we deal with that. Therefore, it's also good that I -- it's a system of tunnels. Yes, okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, first of all, perhaps it's best for the witness to confirm. Am I correct that this is a different tunnel than the one that was under the airport?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was, as I stated in my earlier testimony, the Serbs accused the Bosnians of making tunnels towards their front lines, and the -- this was one of the excuses they used for sniper fire. And I wish to confirm that, in fact, they were making tunnels towards the Bosnian lines, and after being under foot so long on this particular location, the commander, when he knew I was leaving, finally showed me a tunnel which would have allowed about three soldiers abreast to pop up in no man's land to attack position. And the entrance to this tunnel was almost at the very edge of the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I should have known that because Nedzarici is of course not the same as Butmir. That's clear. Please proceed. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can just ask you to clarify, sir, at temporary transcript page 56, line 6, you say "towards the Bosnian lines," am I correct that the tunnel actually went toward the Bosnian Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned the entrance. Was the entrance to this tunnel system camouflaged or masked?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The entrance was masked by a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What kind of building was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was a tall building that was pretty well abandoned and it was right close to the confrontation line. In fact, that's -- that's how they secured it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, could I remind you again about these little pauses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This building that had been abandoned, did it appear to be a civilian-type structure?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make an observation here at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if at the end of your testimony there is a need to add anything to your testimony, you will have an opportunity to do so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but let's focus at this moment on the questions that Mr. Ivetic puts to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to now focus for a few questions on the issue of troop rotations and troop replenishments at the front lines. Would you agree with me that such rotations or movements of troops were a significant strategic phenomena in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: You're asking me to comment on strategy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. Would you agree with me that it is a matter of high military significance to have the ability to move troops in to replenish your front lines and rotate the troops that are located therein, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a -- you want to be able to move your -- that's what harassing fire tries to stop, but if -- it depends on how close they are to the front line, whether it's tactical or operational or if they're far away, strategic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I don't think that harassment fire was part of your question, was it, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It wasn't but I was getting to that. He's anticipating my question, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I would very much like the witness to focus on your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so we can tie the ends together, am I correct that harassing fire would be the targeting of such rotating or moving troops to try to prevent them or at least discourage them from reaching their appointed locations at the front lines?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Not that close to the front lines. You would be firing to either neutralise or destroy them if you were -- if they were close to the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if they were not close to the confrontation line, if they were further in towards the deep territory or towards the residential area of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It depends on obviously to classify -- it depends on when you think the supplies are moving forward. Most usually they are moved at night, usually at a time they don't think that you have visibility on the target area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Based upon your experiences and knowledge, would you agree with me that the Bosnian Presidency forces in Sarajevo had to be moved from more interior positions towards the front lines?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, but they had -- their equipment and ammunition must have been in place because I never once saw them moving with either ammunition or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that such troop movements would likely be accomplished with a certain degree of camouflage such that perhaps even the UNMO mission might miss them?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We rarely missed the movement of that many people moving in some kind of organised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do I recall correctly that one time during the evening you inadvertently come across precisely one such large group of Bosnian Muslim troops advancing towards the front line in new French kit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: In what appears to -- what I assumed was French kit, to make that correction. I've dealt with it and in my testimony. Yes. At night as would be expected, a force of 70 soldiers or more was moving up to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With regard to this kit that appeared to be French, and I guess we should -- for the layperson kit is a uniform and equipment in a military sense?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think -- I think that question about the French kit's already been addressed in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking for clarification.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this equipment, this French -- this seemingly French equipment something you had previously seen among the forces of the Bosnian Presidency in Sarajevo, or did it appear to be newly acquired equipment?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The only thing I can reply to that is exactly what I said in my statement: It was the first time I saw people wearing this equipment turn out to be Bosnians. The rest of your questions, associated questions, I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Would you agree with me there were approximately 25.000 armed Bosnian Presidency soldiers that were located in Sarajevo as part of the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the -- also stated in one of our documents. One of the documents that I provided the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would these men have been legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that some -- many of these men did not wear uniforms or only wore parts of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by the same token, many civilians, including women and elderly and kids, wore uniforms or partial uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that such a situation could cause a degree of confusion in identifying combatants?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge of a significant Mujahedin force of Islamic fighters from outside of Bosnian that were located near Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can return to the document that is still up on our screen in harm's way 1D426, and if I can turn to the fourth page of the document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that sir, I will be asking you about the second to last paragraph of page 2 of the text. It's the bottom of the page. There we go. And I read for you, sir, the quotation I'm interested in: "In Sarajevo itself, a Croatian brigade had responsibility for holding part of the defensive perimeter against the Bosnian Serbs. Only 30 kilometres away in Kiseljak Croatians in that pocket were allied with Bosnian Serbs against Bosnian government forces and were even suspected of lobbing the odd shell into Sarajevo, hitting on occasion other Croats." Now, first of all, sir, is this a true and accurate rendition of the knowledge that you have on this topic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say the Croatians in Kiseljak, am I correct that we're talking about the HVO or the Croat Defence Union as it was called?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: We are talking about what I call Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And the Bosnian Croats were a third party to the conflict, that is to say they had a structure separate and apart from the VRS.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here you identify the force of Croats, the Bosnian Croats, as being allied with the Bosnian Serbs. Would you be surprised to learn that the HVO or Croat Defence Union had previously been considered to be one of the two recognised armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina under the Bosnian Presidency?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about something during the time period that you were there. Are you aware that the United States under the auspices of Ambassador Galbraith brokered the Washington Accords between August of 1993 and February of 1994 to create the so-called Croat-Muslim federation precisely between the Bosnian Croats in Kiseljak and the Bosnian Presidency forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I was aware not that it had been brokered by the United States, but I was aware of an agreement between the Bosnians and Croats in Central Bosnia because I lost some of my team members to go serve there instead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: In -- in February, March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if this shelling by the Croatians in Kiseljak would have occurred before or after that date?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sure it occurred before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here in the article we -- you say that they were "suspected of lobbing the odd shell." Am I correct that it is more than just suspected, that the UNMO mission during your tenure confirmed that the Croatian forces in Kiseljak several times shot heavy weapons that landed inside the Papa side of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. It wasn't UNMO confirmed. The only reason that we suspected was the calibre of round was different, and also there were reports of French guns that were owned by the Croatians in Kiseljak firing, and we made a correlation between the two. So that's why we maintained suspected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I have to ask you to slow down for the interpreters because it's at the speed of speech. So apart from the breaks, small pauses, also to show down your speed of speech, Mr. Ivetic, and if you, in addition, take a bit of a longer pause after that, that would be appreciated. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I will do my best. And I apologise to the translators and to the transcribers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to flesh out your answer a little bit by pulling up 1D424. This is a transcript of your testimony from the Karadzic trial, and I'd like to have page 63 in e-court of this 65 ter document, which should correlate to transcript page 6857 and I'd like to focus on lines 7 through 21. And this is your answer in that proceeding on this topics, sir, and it begins: "We do know that shells fell on the city from Croatian artillery, and that was identified and reported separately. And now I'm surprised to hear from Dr. Karadzic that the Croatians fired on Ilidza, when we, in the year 1993, identified Croatian shells falling on Sarajevo proper. And that isn't in any of the documentation, because it's not part of this investigation. But now that Dr. Karadzic raised Croatian involvement, I feel justified in bringing that point in. "Judge Morrison: What was the frequency of Croatian shelling during your period in Sarajevo? "The witness: The only reason -- not very often. The only reason I remember this distinctly is that when I was trying to explain to people about the convoluted nature of the war in Yugoslavia, I used the example of the Croatians in Kiseljak firing on the Croatians in Sarajevo, because some of the shells fired from Kiseljak which were tracked fell in the city that was being held by Croatian units of the Bosnian forces." First of all, sir, could you confirm for us whether this portion of the testimony from the Karadzic trial is true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you please clarify for me what -- it says here that the shells were tracked. Could you explain for me who tracked the shells?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This is other UNPROFOR units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identify here that this was not in the documentation. Is there -- was there -- was there pressure applied not to record this information in the documentation?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't think so. I learned about it through documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with the incoming rounds from the Croatian artillery coming into Sarajevo be counted in the Increp reports for rounds coming into the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Most likely, but they're so few in number and this particular incident attracted our attention that we probably would have gone out as a team, sent a special team to look at what shells evidence there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified that you were able to determine based upon the type of shell that it was some kind of French artillery that the Croatians had. Could you please give any specifics as to the type of -- the calibre?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I can't, because this was again based on documentation that I saw, not on personal observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness at the time did not fully answer Judge Morrison's question about the frequency. Now he says they were so little in numbers. Could you give us an indication as to what the numbers then were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only -- we only had one incident that we -- came to our attention, but I was told by the people that I asked that there had been other incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And other incidents --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- did they specify whether there were five more or a hundred more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they didn't, but they said there were not very many.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And -- and since there was a United Nations headquarters in Kiseljak, a battery firing there would have been noticeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but whether it was observed you do not know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. But I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could have been observed. You may have missed it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was firing from long range. That's why there was special weapons used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Kiseljak being at what distance approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's over 30 kilometres, but that's off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think the selection we just read had 30 kilometres listed in harm's way was recorded as saying 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that another facet of the convoluted picture of the war in the former Yugoslavia was -- was the ever present rumours and suspicions that the Bosnian Presidency forces shelled their own people in the city, albeit that UNMO during your tenure was never able to confirm such rumours?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, then I think I have to say that it's -- there were rumours about a lot of things, and this is just one of those other rumours we could never confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the UNMO mission --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that the UNMO mission did not have a mandate to perform any thorough criminal investigations into such rumours?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can't speak for the rest of UNPROFOR, but the UNMOs had no mandate to investigate criminal activities, no mandate whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to 1D428 which is again testimony from the Galic proceedings and page 25 in e-court, which ought to correlate to the transcript page 9433. And I'd like to focus on line 13 and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, during this exchange -- well, let me just read it for you: "Q. That is either shot at, wounded or killed by a sniper from the so-called BH army? "A. We assume that he was shot by a sniper from the BH army. We have the same rumours about the Bosnian Serb Army as we have about the Bosnian Army, that sometimes they shot their own people. "Q. I did not ask the question in relation to sniper. So there were rumours, according to you, according to which there were Muslim snipers that were sniping their own people? "A. There were rumours that people were killed by people on their own side for other reasons. "Q. Would those be political reasons, sir? "A. In some cases it was suspected, and other cases [Realtime transcript read in error "case"], criminal activity." Could you first confirm whether this selection I've read is true and accurate.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I was told that temporary transcript page 67, line 10, incorrectly shows "other case" when the selection from the Galic says "cases," plural. Just to complete that record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can focus a little bit on the artillery side. Am I correct that the UNMO mission during your tenure did not have access to the target grids or the maps that were being used by either side to direct their artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, we did not. I assume you are talking about the target maps that they held, not the target maps, because we used the same map sheets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question: Am I correct that the UNMO mission during your tenure did not have access to the target grids and target maps that were being used by the forces to direct their artillery?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that -- well, first of all, in direct you were asked about Canadian artillery and Canadian procedure for calling down artillery. Can we agree that the artillery that was in use around Sarajevo on both sides of the conflict line was not the newer generation artillery used by the United States and its NATO allies? They were not using guided munitions or precision shells but were using more older generation, average-grade weaponry?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: In 1993, the Canadian Forces were using old, average weaponry, and I learned to fire artillery or direct artillery fire using what you call old weapon technology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question about what was available there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the weapons they had there were as good as anything we had in the Canadian army in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that the -- that some NATO countries like the United States have standard operating procedures authorising the use of force even if there is a level of noncombatant injury possible for a given action?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't know about other countries' rules for engaging with artillery fire in the vicinity of noncombatant forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about Canadian? What's the accepted level of collateral damage before an action is taken by the Canadian Armed Forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That has to be taken in context, and we were never in the context of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again a pause between question and answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In a combat such as we were engaged in in World War II, the rules would be completely different than for the rules of something that -- around Sarajevo, but it -- all military observers calling -- all artillery observers calling down artillery fire in the Canadian Forces were trained to be -- recognised the possibility of collateral damage to noncombatants, and they were -- they would be asked to take this into account in their training.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not the catch the last answer by the witness. Could the witness kindly repeat his answer. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- and I do see you have your screen in front of you. If the transcript reflects what you said, could you please then read again from "all artillery observers."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All artillery observers calling down artillery fire in the Canadian Forces were trained to be -- to recognise the possibility of collateral damage to noncombatants, and they would be asked to take this into account in the training and of subsequent targeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you added, the last line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I added the last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Focusing on 1993, and let's focus on the Canadian Armed Forces, am I correct that the use of force could be authorised even for fire missions that included a chance of collateral damage, that is where the likelihood of collateral damage was greater than 0 per cent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I think it would really depend on the context of the situation, how important that objective was, whether they are willing to risk damaging a lot of civilians to achieve that objective, and it's very conjectural. I mean, the -- the experience of the Canadian Forces in places like Ortona found that pounding with artillery fire actually didn't help because it just gave the Germans more cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the decision to authorise use of force, not the effect of the use of force. Would you agree with me that the Canadian Armed Forces of which you have testified about in 1993 authorised included authorisations for the use of force in certain circumstances where there was a risk of actual, verifiable collateral damage taking place?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I specified in combat, which was not the case for Canadian Forces in UNPROFOR, in combat obviously artillery would be authorised to be used but it would always be in the context of the situation. So a specific situation. Unless you were to detail the specific situation, and that would be one of the challenges in training young officers what -- I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the point you apparently want to make is clear. I'm not anticipating on how you [sic] appreciate it, but the point you want to make it clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript says "you appreciate." It is "how we appreciate it." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that another potential source of collateral damage is when it's unplanned, when it is the result of failed positive identification of a target?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm starting to get into the area of speculation, Your Honour. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's more we are talking about theory rather than at this moment, isn't it, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At this point we're talking about general and theory, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's try to return to the facts primarily and there always will be some judgement implied in it, but if we start with the facts then it's better to have some judgement in it, rather than to start with theory and judgement and then to come across a fact now and then. But I leave it in your hands at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We will get to the precise references in his statement as to something similar later in my questioning. I'd like to move now to your written statement, which is Exhibit P503, and I'd like to first look at paragraph 49, which would be on page 11 of the same in English and page 13 of the same in B/C/S. And here you are talking about the Bosnian Serb soldiers and that they were mostly former Territorial Defence soldiers and that the officers had to exert supervision on these men to follow their instructions because they were not working professionals. Would you agree with me based upon your interactions with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that the number of officers who could exert supervision over such nonprofessional soldiers in the Bosnian Serb Army was limited or inadequate?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At this time I'd like to ask you to comment upon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, again if you ask whether the numbers were limited or inadequate, what I'd like to know is what the witness knows about the numbers rather than to first elicit his judgement on whether it was limited or inadequate, but rather to ask him whether he knows how many professionals officers were they aware of, for example, so as to then move to conclusions preferably to be drawn by the Chamber, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you answer the Judge's question? Do you know how many professional officers there were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps during the time period that you were the SMO?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I don't know how many. I only know that the army acted as if they had a professional officer directing them because they did what they were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Wouldn't you be speculating now, sir?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, you asked me the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the issue is that sometimes people who are not professionals are still doing what they were told, and sometimes the instructions are given by persons who are not professionals either. What Mr. Ivetic is asking you when he says are you not speculating, that you are drawing all kind of conclusions on -- I wouldn't say on a wrong factual basis but at least unclear factual basis and that is what Mr. Ivetic draws your attention to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then I can rephrase that. I would say that the -- there seemed to be people with the skill sets that could call down artillery fire accurately and direct fire base unit -- fire units, perhaps more in the Bosnian Serb Army than there were in the Bosnian Army in my -- based on my experience of seeing them in action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to present you with 1D00390, and page 22 of the same in e-court. This is from the Karadzic proceedings and it is something that is the testimony of a Colonel Richard Mole, who was one of your predecessors at the SMO position who served in 1992, and this, once it comes up, should correlate to transcript page 5901. Page 22 of this exhibit. And I'd like to focus on line 5 through 12: "Q. Do you agree that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps had inherited territorial and municipal armies that were already in existence, and everyone, from General Sipcic to General Milosevic, had great problems establishing a unified command structure over these local units? "A. It was certainly a significant difficulty which I observed that both sides had. This was not a unique experience from the Serb side. So I understand what you're saying. I was sympathetic to that situation, and I agree with your overall assessment." Sir, did you observe or were you aware of this problem that your predecessor acknowledged?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm just not clear why we're relying on a transcript of Mr. Mole's evidence in a prior proceeding. Has this area -- is there evidence in this proceeding on this issue from Mr. Mole?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Then shouldn't we be dealing with what he said in these proceedings and not what he said in some prior proceeding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, as a -- what we're talking about is evidence given by another witness either in this case or in another case, and I think Mr. Ivetic can ask questions whether a person who has held a similar position, whether his assessment of the situation, whether this witness agrees with that, yes or no. Therefore, I think it's -- I wouldn't immediately know whether it was exactly -- whether we have similar evidence in this case. I would have to check that first. But there's no problem in asking the question as you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't -- I didn't I think express my objection very well. It seems to me that it's inappropriate -- I don't know what Mr. Mole had to say in these proceedings, but let's assume for a moment that maybe he said something different in these proceedings. You're now being basically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in re-examination, you can address that matter. There's no problem about that. I ruled on the basis of your initial objections that the witness may answer the question and that ruling stands. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mole was ahead of me in Sarajevo, and perhaps the fact that I found fewer skill sets among the Bosnian commanders than the Serb commands reflects the fact that the Bosnian Serb commanders had more skill sets and were able to achieve a greater unified force more quickly. The second point I'd like to make for the edification of the Judges is that artillery units and armoured units which the Bosnian Serbs had which the other Bosnians did not have in large numbers require a skill set which precludes more discipline and working together. Therefore, I would not agree by the time I took over in October 1993 that both sides were having equal difficulty in managing their territorial call-up assets. Do you want me to repeat that for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think they -- yes. The interpretation has now finished. There is a small problem, Mr. Ivetic. The -- what you read to the witness was first about a problem. The witness says that witness said recognises, and then he added to that that it was equal on both sides. Now, apparently the witness focused very much on the equality, and that is the result of you not splitting up the two elements of that answer. You may proceed, and if you want to explore it further, please feel free to do so. If not, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with the assessment or did you have information similar to Colonel Mole that the -- that there were great problems in establishing a unified command structure over local units?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. I disagree, and I -- on several points. Personally, I based my assessment on meeting local commanders and on the situation that I saw happening in real live incidents and not on what other people's reports said about these commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we can -- if we can move to one more aspect of Colonel Mole's testimony, and this is in 1D00389. And it's from the Karadzic proceedings and should be page 78 in the e-court system which, hopefully, if my math is right will correlate to page 5878 from the Karadzic case, and I'd like to focus on lines 13 through 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I have an issue to raise. Is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- I first wanted to give an opportunity, at least the numbers mentioned by Mr. Ivetic to be heard, to be translated, and I was aware that you were on your feet, Ms. Bolton. What is it that you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to know if this portion of the transcript that my friend is going to put to this witness from Mr. Mole's prior testimony was put to Mr. Mole during cross-examination, because if it wasn't, it would violate the rule in Brown v. Dunn that in essence you have to confront the witness who is testifying with what appears to be something he has said before and give him the opportunity to explain, in fairness. So I'd like to know if this passage was put to Mr. Mole before we go any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, Brown v. Dunn is not jurisdiction here. This exact passage was presented to Colonel Mole which he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would agree with Mr. Ivetic that -- now let me -- Ms. Bolton, any further response to what Mr. Ivetic said, both in terms of the applicability of Brown v. Dunn? I take it that you wanted to refer to the underlying idea under Brown v. Dunn.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Correct. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or to any case law in this Tribunal, although you failed to refer us to any authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Two issues: One is that if this passage was put to Mr. Mole in this case and he was given the opportunity to comment on it, then I have no difficulty with it. The principle in Brown v. Dunn, I would suggest, is applicable in these proceedings because it is a principle of fairness to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the only comment was not that the principle does not apply but that the Brown v. Dunn does not apply in itself. Let's try not to lose ourselves in these details. Mr. Ivetic, to the extent you could assist the Chamber and Ms. Bolton in the transcript page where it was put to Mr. Mole, because you'll understand that our recollection is insufficient to immediately have it available. But meanwhile --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile you can proceed, and once you have it, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the part that I want to focus in on of this page begins at line 13, and this is Colonel Mole again answering the question from the accused, Karadzic: "I am in my own mind convinced that there was a considerable anti-Serb approach to the conflict within the press and, indeed, beyond it to some quite senior politicians who I met and talked with in Sarajevo." Sir, did you during your tenure witness similar matters as Colonel Mole has identified here, an anti-Serb position within the media and within senior politicians that he -- that were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, because I gave instructions and I followed them myself to all my military observers to pay no attention to the press or to any visiting politicians in what they said or what their attitudes were. They had one boss. That was me. And they were to ignore, completely ignore what press people told them or any outsiders, and in particular politicians and press people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, if you would like to know whether it was put to Mr. Mole, look at page 4374 of the transcript. That's the advantage of electronic systems which allow you to find it very quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honour, for that one. I will get you the other reference for the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If -- and I -- sir, I appreciate that you limited your answer to your military observers. I'd like to turn back to 1D426, the publication "In Harm's Way."

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And page 8 in e-court, and the section talking about moral courage, which I would present to you. It's at the second half of the page on the left on the screen: "Moral courage. Moral courage is also a requirement, and for me that meant protecting any UNMO under my command from disciplinary action suggested by higher authorities. Initially, this led to unpleasantness with the sector commander who appeared ready to accept the Bosnian government version of an incident on Mount Igman over the report submitted by one of my observer teams. He wanted the UNMO who filed a report that was contradictory to a Bosnian version to be transferred out of Sector Sarajevo. I refused to do this or to change my situation report (SITREP) to conform to what the sector commander said." First of all, sir, is this selection from your article truthful and accurate, and if asked under oath would you give this same info?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And again, I think we have to wait for the translations and transcribers, so please try to pause after my question. And the sector commander, that would be General Soubirou; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And by the "Bosnian version," are we talking about the Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Presidency side?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, Bosnian version is exactly what it means in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do we -- do you have knowledge of any other instances where senior UN officials sided with the Bosnian Presidency version of incidents that your UNMO observers reported as being factually different from that version?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I didn't worry about it. If I accepted what my UNMOs said was factually correct, I would argue and it didn't make any difference to me whether the senior man disagreed with it because he was pro-Bosnian or pro-Serb, it was whether my guy reported what he saw, and I believe my guy over anybody else's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was whether you have any other examples where this had happened not whether you would -- you would be part of it or whether you noticed it to happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately for the Defence I have an example which is -- shows the other side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the translation has caught up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic, for keeping me on the right track as well. Meanwhile, I put it to the witness that he responded not to your question. You may follow up as you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, irrespective of whether you acted upon complaints, were there other instances where senior UN officials appeared to side with pro-Bosnian Presidency versions of incidents that were in conflict with what the UNMO observers reported as being factually the case?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: None that I can recall right now. The only one I recall was the exact opposite of the case you just presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm looking at the clock. It would be time for a "pauze."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We could take a break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last word was "pauze." I noticed that. We -- could first we have the witness escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, we will resume at 25 minutes past 6.00, but could I ask you as well to -- whether you are on track, because there's this specific agreement between the parties that we would conclude the testimony of this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How much time will we have after the break? It's -- 35. I'll be close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, in view of the witness to appear tomorrow, is there any flexibility possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so -- I think Your Honour's recollection of the agreement is different, and since Mr. Stojanovic was here and I think Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Lukic were not here. I thought that what Mr. Stojanovic said that we -- they may request the first session tomorrow but even with that, they would complete the examination of the next witness by the end of the day tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I missed that. So there is some flexibility. There seems to be no major problem at this moment. We take the break and we resume at 25 minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we wait for the witness, I could give the transcript reference for the Colonel Mole testimony. It was transcript page 46 -- 4363, line 23 to 4364, line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. I used the time for the following instruction to the Registry in relation to the D40 and D42, both MFI'd. The Defence has provided revised versions for MFIs D40 and D42, and the Registry may make the necessary replacements and then D40 and D42 are admitted into evidence. I take it that they have been provided to the Prosecution, the new versions. If not, we'll hear from Mr. Groome very soon, isn't it Mr. Groome? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I hope he has more information than I do on that matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If it's not too soon, we have not received it. We would appreciate a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if there's any problem with the new versions, Mr. Groome, then we would like to hear from you, well, let's say within the next two or three days. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 1D423.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for that, Mr. Thomas, this is a document that was disclosed to us by the Prosecution, which purports to be the information report of their -- oops. There it is. Information report of their proofing session with General Sir Michael Rose on the 29th of August, 2003 at the Ministry of Defence, London, United Kingdom. And I'd like focus on page 3 in e-court, bottom of the page. And the part I'd like to ask you about, sir, reads as follows: "I am sure that the Serbs were firing at the trams, but I believe Ganic also organised his secret police to snipe trams. His sniper units sniped so that the angle of the shot matched the direction of the Serb line. During long cease-fires I think that Ganic and the Muslims were responsible for breaking the cease-fire. This kept the tension." Sir, at the time that your UNMO mission was responding to and looking into sniping incidents, did you have knowledge of either this belief of General Rose or any underlying information that the Bosnian Presidency secret police snipers were sniping at trams in a way to match the direction of the Serb line?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the only sniper position that you actually visited on the Bosnian Muslim side was in fact under the control of the police rather than the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that your visit to this Bosnian Presidency sniping unit, which was under police control, was in part -- in furtherance of an investigation into repeated Serb complaints of incoming fire from this location?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that your investigation found this Bosnian Muslim police sniping unit located inside a building that was a school or that had been a school?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was the school still in use or had it -- or was it solely occupied by this unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: It was solely occupied by this unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I've seen witnesses here before who were not so eager to immediately answer the question, so apart from making a pause, I would say just take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, as a military officer, if a school such as this one was being used by a unit of police snipers and was no longer a functioning school, would it constitute a legitimate target for the opposing force?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, the fact it was almost on the front lines would have precluded it being used as a school anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you consider it unusual and in fact worrisome that the sniper activity of the Bosnian Muslim side seemed to be under the control of the police rather than the army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 4 in e-court of General Rose's proofing note or information sheet, and it's the bottom of the page again. And here General Rose is talking about the UNMO mission, and according to this document from the Prosecution, he says: "The UNMO reports were completely useless. It was a money-spinner. They wrote shoot-reps and reports based on what they were told by the local commanders. Many were not technically competent and some were sold out. They were captured by the ones they were there with." Now, sir, to be fair, I did want to advise you - and we can go to the next page in the English - that there is an assessment of yourself by General Rose, and he states as follows: "Thomas was an excellent UNMO, very hard working and committed." So you have the full picture of this assessment. I'd like to focus on the negative comments of General Rose and ask you, do you agree with the assertion that many of the UNMOs were not technically competent?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I completely disagree with this statement about the UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take it step-by-step, sir, and I'll give you the opportunity to respond. Do you agree with the assertion that some of the UNMOs were "sold out"?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with the -- part of the assessment that said that the UNMOs sided with whomever they were situated with and that reports were based on what local commanders told them rather than the facts they observed?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No. You just brought up an incident where they disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm close to the point that I have to work as a traffic policeman, saying, Now you. Now you. Try to do it yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct that there were -- there was at least one incident that you became aware of later where some of your UNMO staff who had violated your instruction not to fraternise with the locals had in fact become involved with a Bosnian Muslim female and had violated regulations to transport them out of a particular zone?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes. And the fact is the UNMO that assisted him, I got him fired out of Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, was that particular instance the only instance of that type of thing that you were aware of during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How many other such instances of that type of behaviour were you aware of?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I can -- I can -- I can't recall now, but I can -- at least three other incidents come to mind, some of which were revealed to me after I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but these -- this is a question of personal -- it doesn't involve either any of the allegations of General Rose about money spinning or false reports. This is someone being involved with one of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you've answered the question, and let's leave it to that, because you are giving additional comments which you consider to be relevant, and in this courtroom we leave it to the parties and to the Bench to decide what we consider to be relevant enough to ask questions about. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that due to the manner in which the observation locations were set up, that on the Serb side of the confrontation line the casualties were not adequately covered by the reports?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I would agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- and am I correct that the Bosnian Muslim or Presidency forces held -- held a position on Mount Igman where they had heavy weapons located?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: They only had 120-millimetre mortars during my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did -- did you or your mission ever have access to the entirety of the Mount Igman portion held by the Presidency forces during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I clarify the question? Is he talking about -- are you talking about the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you can ask to clarify the question if you do not fully understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you talking about after the cease-fire when weapons were being collected?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: And I have already testified, no, we were not allowed access to the Bosnian weapons that they held on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the Serb side complain to you of the Muslim heavy weapons firing upon them from this area of Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: As I already stated, during the cease-fire, I didn't have any weapons, heavy weapons, fired by either side. So it would have taken place before the cease-fire. Is that -- does your question apply to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. During the time period when heavy weapons would have been used, did you have complaints from the Serbs as to these particular weapons from the Mount Igman location being used to direct fire upon them?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, against military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You testified in direct examination about a military offensive in, I believe, it was August that was in the Igman area, and you identified that your information second-hand was that General Mladic commanded this offensive. Could you give us the details precisely when, in what form, and where General Mladic -- where General Mladic would have -- would have planned this offensive based upon the second-hand information that you had?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I can't. I was doing another job at the time in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask you to pause a little more, I think that would help with the other people that need to work in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your second-hand information as to the offensive at Mount Igman identify the Bosnian Presidency forces that were engaged in combat counter to this offensive?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move on then. At paragraph 88 of your amalgamated statement, which would be P503, page 19 in the English and page 23 in the B/C/S, you talk about an incident on 13 October 1993, where Bosnian soldiers disguised themselves as Serbs and shot at the BH commander. First of all, was this the only incident that you had knowledge of where Bosnian Presidency forces impersonated Serb troops?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only incident I had knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information or assessment of the intended object of this action?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we look at paragraph 87 on the same page in both versions of your amalgamated statement, you identify the removal of some Bosnian Presidency commanders who were a criminal element, including Celo, C-e-l-o. I'd like to get some more details. According to your information, how many such commanders were there on the Bosnian Presidency side whom you would label as a criminal element?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't have any idea how many I would label, because I didn't know enough about them privately, but the people that in my -- in my statement, I identified the commanders that were relieved of their duties and also the details of their relief -- relieving them of their duties is not known because it took combat action to relieve them in some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when you say it took combat action to relieve them in some cases, am I correct that you're talking about conflict between -- between two elements of the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: The government of -- the Bosnian government forces had to use force to remove these commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these commanders that they had to use force to remove were their own commanders?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another topic now. At paragraph 19 of your amalgamated statement, which is back on page 5 in the English and page 6 in the B/C/S, you identify one of the duties of the UNMOs being to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid. How often were your UNMOs called upon to fulfil this task in addition to their observation task?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS ROY THOMAS
utterances.text: This is more complex than a yes or no answer. Do I have permission to go ahead? Well, first of all, we had the most up-to-date information, so the humanitarian aid agencies came to my headquarters and asked us for information and to have that information on -- that we have displayed on our map, to have access to that. In the case of Gorazde, I had to substitute military observer convoy -- as convoy escorts when the permission for the French escort was denied from by Pale. We also had to evacuate a casualty, a sick person from the Sarajevo hospital from Gorazde using a military observer vehicle when air-lift was denied access. We basically tried to avoid any escort of humanitarian delivery because we were not armed, and some of the country's drivers refused to drive in a convoy which did not have an armoured ambulance, which of course I did not have an armoured ambulance. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't think you answered the question, Mr. Thomas. The question is how often, not to detail what you told -- or I can read the question to you. It says: "How often were your UNMOs called upon to fulfil this task in addition to their observation tasks?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say, Your Honour, we did it every day. Every day I was in Sarajevo we had an NGO or humanitarian aid agency --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You answered me. You did it every day. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Were the staff that were called upon to fulfil the task of facilitating the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
